name: Testicular sun / red light exposure

lead: Biohackers expose the scrotum to sunlight or to red or near-infrared lamps, hoping to raise testosterone for more muscle, drive and masculine presence. It circulates in biohacking circles and occasionally on looksmaxxing forums.

Proponents say light stimulates Leydig cells or mitochondria in testicular tissue, which they associate with testosterone production. Red-light therapy (photobiomodulation) is studied for pain and wound problems, but the sources reviewed do not describe testicular effects, and no human trials were found for testosterone, fertility or appearance.

paras: People use brief sessions of direct sun or a red-light lamp aimed at the area, often as part of a wider morning-light or biohacking routine. Users generally continue for weeks and compare energy and bloodwork.

The scrotum keeps the testes a few degrees below core temperature, and higher temperatures are reported to impair spermatogenesis. Lamps or sun can add heat and skin exposure risks such as burns. Light therapy devices are cleared by the FDA only for specific uses, and none are cleared for this one.

angle.text: Biohackers shine sunlight or red light on the testes, hoping to stimulate testosterone for muscle and masculine drive. It is a fringe practice, and no human trials were found.

lead: Testicular sun or red light exposure, nicknamed "testicle tanning" in media coverage, is a practice in which men expose the scrotum to sunlight or to red or near-infrared lamps in the hope of raising testosterone. Proponents link higher testosterone with the things many men want to see in the mirror: more muscle, leaner body composition, more energy to train and a more masculine overall look, so the practice is discussed in biohacking circles and occasionally in looksmaxxing hormone-optimisation threads.[1][2]

The idea drew wide attention in April 2022 when Andrew McGovern, a personal trainer, promoted infrared light on the scrotum on Tucker Carlson's Fox News special The End of Men, where he called it "bromeotherapy".[3] Proponents also point to a 1939 study of a handful of hospitalised men and to a small unpublished conference study.[4]

Red and near-infrared light applied to the body is studied as photobiomodulation for conditions such as pain and wound healing, and a 2023 paper examined photobiomodulation and human sperm function in the lab.[5] Urologists quoted in media say they know of no data showing that light on the testes raises testosterone, and they note the testes are normally kept cooler than the body, with heat associated with reduced sperm quality.[3][4][6]
infobox: Sunlight or red/near-infrared lamp on the scrotum

paras: Practitioners describe exposing the scrotal area to sunlight outdoors or to a red or near-infrared panel for short sessions. The reasoning offered is that light reaches testicular tissue and stimulates testosterone-producing cells.[3][4]
A related variant, perineal sunning, is promoted on social media as an ancient Taoist practice, according to Skeptic magazine's review.[4]

Proponents cite a 1939 study by Myerson and Neustadt of five hospitalised men with depression, which measured androsterone, a testosterone metabolite, after light exposure. Skeptic magazine notes the reported increase was smaller than popular summaries claim.[4] Inverse describes the same idea as tracing to a 1939 study of about eight men without a control group, as noted by UCLA urologist Jesse Mills, and never replicated.[3]

A second cited source is a small conference study by Andrea Fagiolini in men with low sexual desire, which reportedly found testosterone rising from 2.3 to 3.6 ng/mL and was not published in a peer-reviewed journal.[4]
The practice reached mainstream audiences through the April 2022 Fox News special, after which many outlets published expert reactions.[3][4]

Photobiomodulation applies low-power lasers or LEDs to tissue. Its history includes Niels Finsen's red-light work in the early twentieth century and Endre Mester's 1960s laser experiments.[1] Evidence is described as mixed, with tentative support for some pain conditions and weaker results for others, and light penetrates only to limited depths.[1]

The scrotum holds the testes about two or three degrees Celsius below core body temperature, and higher temperatures affect spermatogenesis.[2] Another reference describes sperm production as impeded above roughly 36.7 degrees Celsius and says Leydig cells make testosterone under control of luteinizing hormone from the pituitary.[6]

Urologist Ashley Winter said there is no data on testicle tanning and that light would not reach the testes to stimulate testosterone.[3] Jesse Mills noted that testosterone levels can swing by around 100 points in a day, so a later test can look higher without any treatment, and that heat can harm sperm.[3] The Skeptic review reports that urologists found no scientific evidence for the claim and that the Cleveland Clinic found insufficient evidence for most red light therapy uses and none for raising testosterone.[4]

Because testicular heat is associated with impaired spermatogenesis, heat from lamps or direct sun is a concern for fertility.[2][6] Skin burns are a general risk of heat or sun exposure to sensitive skin. Light therapy devices cleared by the FDA are cleared for specific uses, and the FDA has taken action against a device maker over claims of treating hundreds of diseases.[1]

Related research includes a 2023 laboratory study of photobiomodulation and human sperm function, red-light therapy trials for other conditions, and studies of heat effects on spermatogenesis, but none tests light applied to the testes for testosterone.[5][1][2]

lore.intro: Proponents in biohacking and some looksmaxxing circles discuss light on the testes as a low-cost testosterone aid, and media coverage since 2022 has recorded both the claims and clinicians' responses.[3][4]
